summary: This standards-track document defines an Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP) extension for managing domain name registrations and applications while a domain registry is launching. It lets registrars handle special launch periods, such as pre-registration phases, through EPP. It builds on the standard EPP domain mapping.

plainLanguage.summary: When a new toy goes on sale, there is often a special early line. This describes how shops talk to the registry during such a special early period for domain names.

how do registrars handle domain name launch periods

what is a trademark claims notice
what are launch application statuses in epp
subtitle: How a domain registry's EPP interface handles sunrise, landrush and trademark claims periods at launch.

tldr.problem: When a domain registry launches, it runs special phases with rules that differ from steady-state registration, such as several competing applications for one name and trademark checks. The standard EPP domain mapping was designed for steady-state operation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines an EPP extension, in the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:launch-1.0, that adds a launch phase, application identifiers, launch statuses, trademark claims and mark validation to the existing domain commands.
tldr.outcome: Registrars get one uniform interface for Launch Applications and Launch Registrations. Which phases, forms and validators a registry supports stays a matter of server policy.

today: RFC 8334 is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the EPP domain name mapping of RFC 5731 and works with the mark objects of RFC 7848.

sections.title: Why Launches Need an Extension
sections.content:
RFC 8334 describes an extension mapping for version 1.0 of the Extensible Provisioning Protocol (EPP, RFC 5730). It covers the provisioning and management of domain name registrations and applications while a registry is launching.

The text calls such a period a launch phase. Registries often operate in special modes then, with special rules for allocating names. The EPP domain name mapping (RFC 5731) is designed for steady-state operation, so the model during launch may differ from it.

Two terms matter throughout. A Launch Registration is made when the server uses a first-come, first-served model, so only one registration for a name can exist at a time. A Launch Application is an intent to register a name when the server accepts many applications for the same name and later picks one to allocate. RFC 7848 defines a registry interface for the Trademark Claims phase, and this extension sits beside it. Server policy decides what is supported, and the RFC says that policy is typically communicated out of band.
sections.plainLanguage: Opening day at a new shop works differently from a normal day. Sometimes several people ask for the same item and the shop picks one later. This document gives the shopkeepers a common way to handle that.

sections.title: Launch Phases and Validators
sections.content:
A client MUST include a <launch:phase> element to say which phase a command targets. The server SHOULD check it against its active phase and MAY check the optional sub-phase, returning EPP error code 2306 on a mismatch. The name attribute holds a sub-phase, or the full phase name when the value is custom.

The RFC defines five phase values: sunrise (trademark holders submit registrations or applications with verifiable trademark information), landrush (a later phase for non-trademark holders, with steps to cope with a large volume of early registrations), claims (a claims notice must be shown to a prospective registrant whose name matches a trademark), open (also called steady state) and custom. Phases MAY overlap. Claims and landrush overlapping SHOULD be written as <launch:phase name='landrush'>claims</launch:phase>.

Trademark data comes from a Trademark Validator, named by the optional validatorID attribute. The ICANN Trademark Clearinghouse (TMCH) is the default and is reserved for the identifier tmch. A server using other or multiple validators MUST list its supported identifiers and publish them out of band. A validator may also support kinds of claims beyond trademarks.
sections.plainLanguage: A launch has stages, like early access for ticket holders and then a big rush for everyone. Each message says which stage it is for, and a trusted referee, called a validator, checks that a trademark claim is real.

sections.title: The Trademark Claims Flow
sections.content:
In the claims phase the client talks to three parties: the server, a Claims Notice Information Service (CNIS, which may be linked to a Trademark Validator) and the registrant. First the client does a normal domain check. If the name is available, it sends a Claims Check, which does not report availability. Instead the response says, through an exists attribute on each name, whether at least one matching trademark exists that requires the Claims Create Form.

When a trademark matches, the response carries one or more <launch:claimKey> elements. The client passes the key to the validator to fetch the information for a Trademark Claims Notice. The key stands in for the domain name so the query does not use a well-known value. The client displays the notice. If the registrant acknowledges it, the client sends a create command carrying a <launch:notice> with the noticeID, notAfter and acceptedDate values. If the registrant does not acknowledge, the flow aborts.

There is also an Availability Check form (type='avail') that asks about availability in a given phase, and a Trademark Check form (type='trademark') that reports matching trademarks regardless of the active phase.
sections.plainLanguage: Before you can claim a name that looks like a famous brand, you get a warning label to read. You show you read it, and only then can you sign up for the name.

sections.title: Application and Registration Status
sections.content:
A Launch Application or Registration MAY carry a <launch:status> value, given in the required s attribute. While the launch status is supported and is not a final one, the object MUST hold the EPP pendingCreate status.

  • pendingValidation: the initial state, validation not yet complete.
  • validated: meets the registry rules.
  • invalid: fails validation. Server policy permitting, it may return to pendingValidation after corrections.
  • pendingAllocation: waiting on an out-of-band process such as an auction.
  • allocated and rejected: the two possible end states.
  • custom: a server-defined status named by the name attribute.

Transitions are a matter of server policy, and the RFC gives one possible set in a diagram. Statuses MAY be skipped, so an object can start at allocated, or go straight to pendingAllocation when no validation is needed. The server SHOULD use the non-custom values.

As an object moves through statuses, the server SHOULD insert EPP poll messages for the intermediate ones. For the final statuses it MUST insert a <domain:panData> poll message.
sections.plainLanguage: An application is like a parcel being tracked. It starts at being checked, may be approved, may wait for a final decision, and ends up either accepted or turned down.

sections.title: Mark Validation Models
sections.content:
A server MUST support at least one of four ways to validate trademark information.

  • code: a mark code alone, sent in <launch:codeMark> with only <launch:code>.
  • mark: the mark information alone, which the server validates with some custom form of validation.
  • code with mark: a secret code plus the mark data, so the server can validate with an external party.
  • signed mark: the mark data is digitally signed, using <smd:signedMark> or <smd:encodedSignedMark>. The server can check the signature with the public key of the party that signed it, and when digital signatures are used the server MUST validate them.

More than one mark element MAY be sent for a name. The maximum number of marks per domain name is server policy. The mark and signed mark elements are defined in RFC 7848, and new formats can be added by defining an XML schema with a substituting element.
sections.plainLanguage: To prove a name is really yours, you can show a secret code, show your trademark paperwork, show both, or show paperwork with an official stamp that the shop can check.

sections.title: Extending the EPP Commands
sections.content:
Operations use the existing domain commands of RFC 5731, and registries MAY support a subset. The extension adds elements to each:

  • check: three forms, chosen by the type attribute: claims (the default), avail and trademark. A server MUST return error 2307 for an unsupported form.
  • info: <launch:info> with the phase, an optional applicationID and an includeMark attribute (default false) asking for the marks back.
  • create: four forms. Sunrise carries verifiable marks, Claims carries the notice acceptance, General only names the phase and optional object type, and Mixed combines forms (the custom phase SHOULD be used with it). On success the server MAY return <launch:creData> with the application identifier.
  • update and delete: they act on an application by its applicationID. A server without Launch Applications MUST return error 2102.
  • renew and transfer: no extension is defined.

When a server accepts several applications for one name, it assigns an application identifier on create, sets pendingCreate, and all later operations on that application MUST use the identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: The normal forms for asking a registry about a name get extra boxes to tick, such as which stage you are in and which application you mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extension provides no security services beyond those of EPP (RFC 5730), the domain mapping (RFC 5731) and the protocol layers EPP runs over. Their security considerations apply here as well.

Updates to and deletion of an application object MUST be restricted to authorized clients. The RFC notes that the content of an application, or even the fact that it exists, may be confidential. An unauthorized attempt to operate on an application MUST be rejected with EPP code 2201. If server policy lets other clients run info, the <domain:infData> and <launch:infData> responses SHOULD be filtered to publicly accessible fields.
sections.plainLanguage: Your application is private. Only the shop that sent it may change or cancel it, and strangers who ask get turned away or see only the public bits.
